_note: Omnisciente assessment guidance for CIS Controls v8.1 IG1. Practical verification prompts, not CIS text; they do not change or add safeguard requirements. 'stack' names Client Profile security technology that may indicate a capability exists; it never establishes implementation.

checks: An authoritative inventory exists and names its source (RMM, MDM, directory, discovery).
Coverage includes servers, end-user devices, network, mobile, cloud and remote assets.
Each asset has an owner, identifier and authorization status.
Additions and retirements are reconciled on a defined schedule.
The last reconciliation is dated within the six-month cycle.
Unknown devices are detected (discovery scan, NAC, DHCP or EDR reports).
A defined response exists: remove, block, isolate or authorize.
Recent unknown-device cases show a decision and closure date.
The process runs at least weekly.
A software inventory exists with its collection source.
Entries record publisher, version, business purpose and owner.
Cloud/SaaS applications are included, not only installed software.
The inventory was reviewed within the six-month cycle.
Support status is known for authorized software.
Unsupported software is removed or has an approved, dated exception.
Exceptions record compensating controls and a review date.
Support status is checked monthly.
Unauthorized software can be identified from the inventory or tooling.
Detected software is removed or formally authorized.
Recent cases show resolution, not only detection.
Review occurs at least monthly.
A data management process is documented and approved.
It assigns data owners and covers sensitivity, handling, retention and disposal.
It was reviewed within the last year or after significant change.
Sensitive data locations and owners are inventoried.
SaaS repositories (M365, file shares, line-of-business apps) are included.
The inventory was updated within the last year.
Access to sensitive repositories is restricted by role or need.
Permission exports match the documented access model.
Broad groups (Everyone, external sharing links) are identified and justified.
Retention periods are defined for each data category.
Retention is enforced by configuration or a performed process.
Records show deletion actually occurs at end of retention.
A disposal method is defined for data and media.
Disposal records identify what was destroyed, how and by whom.
Third-party destruction certificates are retained where used.
Encryption is enforced by policy on laptops and mobile devices.
A coverage report shows the encrypted percentage of the fleet.
Unencrypted exceptions are identified and tracked.
Recovery keys are escrowed and access-controlled.
Documented configuration baselines exist for workstations and servers.
Baselines are deployed by tooling, not only documented.
Compliance reporting identifies drifted or non-compliant assets.
Baselines were reviewed within the last year.
Configuration standards exist for firewalls, switches and wireless.
Changes follow a recorded change process.
Device configurations are backed up and compared to standard.
Standards were reviewed within the last year.
Session lock is enforced: ≤15 minutes for OS, ≤2 minutes for mobile.
The setting is applied by policy across the fleet.
Exceptions are identified with justification.
Host firewalls are enabled on servers.
Rule sets default-deny and are documented.
Exceptions and open ports have an owner and justification.
Host firewall is enforced on end-user devices by policy.
Default-deny with only required exceptions.
Coverage report shows no disabled firewalls.
Administrative interfaces use secure protocols (SSH, HTTPS).
Insecure management protocols (Telnet, HTTP) are disabled.
Infrastructure-as-code or management tooling is access-controlled.
Default accounts are disabled, renamed or have changed credentials.
Network devices, applications and cloud services are included.
A recent check confirms no default credentials remain.
An account inventory covers user, admin and service accounts.
Each account has an owner, purpose and start date.
The inventory is validated at least quarterly against HR records.
Password policy requires unique passwords (8+ with MFA, 14+ without).
Technical enforcement exists in the identity provider.
Shared credentials are eliminated or held in a managed vault.
Accounts inactive for 45 days are disabled where supported.
The check is automated or recorded as a performed task.
Recent results show dormant accounts actually disabled.
Administrators use dedicated privileged accounts.
Admin accounts are not used for email or browsing.
A current list of privileged accounts is reviewed and justified.
Access is granted through a documented request and approval.
Recent new hires or role changes show approval before access.
Access granted matches the approved request.
Access is revoked promptly at termination or role change.
Recent leavers show disablement on or before the last day.
Revocation covers SaaS and third-party accounts, not only the directory.
MFA is enforced for all externally-exposed applications.
Enforcement is by conditional access or equivalent, not user choice.
Excluded accounts and legacy protocols are identified and justified.
VPN and remote access require MFA.
No remote access path bypasses MFA.
Configuration evidence shows enforcement.
All administrative access requires MFA.
Break-glass accounts are documented, protected and monitored.
Admin portals and cloud consoles are included.
A vulnerability management process is documented.
It defines scan scope, frequency and severity-based timelines.
It was reviewed within the last year.
Remediation timelines are defined by severity.
Open vulnerabilities are tracked to closure or exception.
Monthly review shows timelines are being met.
OS patching is automated for workstations and servers.
Patch compliance reporting is reviewed monthly.
Devices failing to patch are identified and remediated.
Third-party application patching is automated.
Coverage includes browsers, PDF readers and common runtimes.
Compliance reporting identifies outdated applications.
A logging process defines what is collected, retained and reviewed.
Responsibility for log review is assigned.
The process was reviewed within the last year.
Audit logging is enabled on identity, endpoint and key systems.
Collection matches the logging process scope.
A sample confirms logs are actually being generated.
Log storage meets the defined retention period.
Storage capacity is monitored.
Retention settings are confirmed in configuration.
Only supported browsers and email clients are permitted.
Versions are managed and kept current.
Unsupported versions are identified in inventory.
DNS filtering is applied to enterprise assets.
Coverage extends to remote and off-network devices.
Blocked-category and exception reports are reviewed.
Anti-malware/EDR is deployed on all supported assets.
Deployment coverage reconciles to the asset inventory.
Unprotected or offline agents are identified and resolved.
Signature and engine updates are automatic.
Agents reporting stale definitions are identified.
Update status is monitored centrally.
Autorun and autoplay are disabled by policy.
The setting is applied across the fleet.
Exceptions are documented.
A data recovery process is documented with scope and priorities.
Recovery objectives are defined for critical systems.
The process was reviewed within the last year.
Backups are automated for in-scope systems and SaaS data.
Frequency matches data sensitivity (weekly or more often).
Failed jobs are monitored and resolved.
A restore test confirms backups are usable.
Recovery data is protected (encryption, access control).
Backup administration is restricted to named individuals.
Backup deletion requires elevated approval or is immutable.
An isolated or offline copy of recovery data exists.
Isolation is technical (immutable, air-gapped or separate tenant).
Isolation is confirmed in configuration, not assumed.
Network infrastructure runs supported, current firmware.
Firmware and software updates are reviewed monthly.
End-of-life devices have a replacement plan.
A security awareness program is defined and owned.
Training occurs at hire and at least annually.
Completion rates are tracked; non-completion is followed up.
Content was reviewed within the last year.
Training covers phishing, pretexting and tailgating.
Phishing simulations or equivalent measure effectiveness.
Completion is recorded.
Training covers MFA, password composition and credential management.
Completion is recorded.
Training covers identifying, storing, transferring and disposing of sensitive data.
Content aligns with the data management process (3.1).
Completion is recorded.
Training covers misdelivery, loss of devices and unintended publishing.
Completion is recorded.
Training explains how to recognize and report incidents.
The reporting channel in training matches the current process (17.3).
Completion is recorded.
Training explains how to confirm and report missing security updates.
Completion is recorded.
Training covers risks of public and untrusted networks.
Guidance on VPN or approved connectivity is included.
Completion is recorded.
A service provider inventory exists with classification and owner.
Providers handling sensitive data are identified.
The inventory reconciles to the Vendor Register.
It was reviewed within the last year.
A named person and backup manage incident handling.
Responsibilities are documented and acknowledged.
The designation was reviewed within the last year.
Incident contacts (internal, legal, insurer, law enforcement, MSP) are current.
Contact details were verified within the last year.
The list is accessible during an outage.
A documented process tells workforce how and to whom to report incidents.
The process is communicated and accessible.
It was reviewed within the last year.
